one_liner: nanobench's built-in RomuDuoJr generator: a drop-in <random>-style 64-bit PRNG, ~1.3-3.9x faster than std::mt19937_64.
what_it_does: Ships inside the nanobench header-only microbenchmarking library as ankerl::nanobench::Rng, a 64-bit generator satisfying the UniformRandomBitGenerator shape (operator(), result_type, min()/max()), so it plugs into std::uniform_int_distribution and similar STL machinery in place of std::mt19937/mt19937_64. It also adds non-standard helpers std engines lack: bounded(range) for fast ranged integers, uniform01() for a fast [0,1) double, and shuffle(container) as a faster std::shuffle replacement. It exists to generate benchmark inputs quickly so the RNG itself doesn't distort the measurement.
how_it_is_fast: Implements RomuDuoJr (Mark Overton's Romu family), a non-cryptographic generator with only 128 bits of state (two uint64_t words) and a per-call update of one 64-bit multiply plus a subtract-then-rotate, far cheaper than Mersenne Twister's large state array and tempering step. operator() is declared inline in the header so it can fully inline at the call site. The design trades statistical rigor and state size for minimal instructions per call.
when_to_use: Feeding random inputs to a nanobench benchmark loop where RNG overhead must stay well below the measured operation's own cost
Non-cryptographic hot loops needing a fast 64-bit value or ranged integer where std::mt19937/mt19937_64 throughput is the bottleneck
Already depending on nanobench and wanting to avoid pulling in a second PRNG library for lightweight randomness
Need a fast, slightly-biased container shuffle (shuffle()) instead of std::shuffle
Deterministic-but-throwaway sequences within a single build (seed via Rng(seed)) where cross-version reproducibility isn't required
when_not_to_use: Anything security- or cryptography-adjacent - the header states outright it is not cryptographically secure
Large-scale simulation or Monte Carlo work - the author's own doc comment caps estimated capacity at ~2^51 bytes and calls it 'not enough for large jobs'
Code that must reproduce the same sequence across nanobench upgrades - the header warns the underlying algorithm may change between releases
Multi-threaded code sharing one generator instance - thread safety isn't documented and Rng is move-only (copy disabled), implying one instance per thread
Workloads needing an unbiased bounded-integer distribution - bounded() uses a fast biased reduction, not rejection sampling

integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMake target_compile_features cxx_std_11; repo advertises C++11/14/17/20 support)
integration.platforms: platform-independent - pure integer/multiply ops, no SIMD or ISA requirement
integration.thread_safety: not documented; Rng is move-only (copy constructor/assignment deleted) and holds unsynchronized mutable state, implying one instance per thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial - explain: matches the UniformRandomBitGenerator interface so it works with std::uniform_int_distribution etc., but unlike std::mt19937_64 it cannot be copied (only moved, or cloned via .copy()) and it adds extra non-standard methods (bounded, uniform01, shuffle, state)

gotchas: Copy constructor and copy-assignment are deleted; use .copy() or move semantics instead of copying by value
The algorithm may change between nanobench releases (documented in the header), so seeded sequences aren't guaranteed stable across upgrades
bounded(range) uses a fast, slightly biased reduction rather than rejection sampling
Using it outside nanobench still requires building the one translation unit compiled with ANKERL_NANOBENCH_IMPLEMENT, like the rest of the header-only library
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only if you're already using nanobench and want a zero-dependency fast RNG for generating benchmark inputs. For general-purpose or higher-throughput random number generation, PCG (pcg-cpp/wjakob pcg32) or xoshiro_cpp are better studied, and the tutorial's own numbers show nanobench::Rng's edge over std::mt19937_64 (~1.3-3.9x, inconsistent across two runs) is smaller and shakier than PCG's (~3.5-4x) or xoshiro256++'s (~3.2x) measured margins.
verified_claims_summary: Nanobench's own tutorial.rst shows two different first-party runs, neither stating compiler, flags, or CPU: a relative()-table run has ankerl::nanobench::Rng at 1.57 ns/uint64_t vs std::mt19937_64 at 2.03 ns (~1.3x) and vs std::default_random_engine at 35.87 ns (~22.8x); a separate compare()-table run (with 95% CI) has nanobench::Rng at 0.49 ns/uint64_t vs std::mt19937 at 1.71 ns (3.48x, CI 3.46-3.50x) and vs std::mt19937_64 at 1.90 ns (~3.9x). The two runs disagree by roughly 3x on the margin over mt19937_64, and the second table's exact RNG lineup (includes an unlabeled 'lcg by hand') has no corresponding source file checked into the repo.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-06) and MIT-licensed; the whole library is one header plus a one-line implementation .cpp, trivial to vendor even if development ever stalls.
